extracted.intended_audience: educators, teachers, educational theorists, and students of education
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical and practical principles for organizing education as continuous growth rather than mere preparation, unfolding, or rote training. Emphasizes habits, plasticity, social nurture, and methods that preserve and extend capacity to learn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education as continuous development (education is its own end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is development; the educational process has no end beyond itself and is one of continual reorganizing, reconstructing, transforming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat schooling merely as preparation for an external goal; design educational experiences so that growing (development) at each stage is the aim in itself. The criterion of school value is how well it creates desire and means for continued growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate plasticity (capacity to learn from experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plasticity is the ability to learn from experience, to retain from prior experience factors that modify subsequent actions — in short, the power to modify actions on the basis of past results and 'learn to learn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should cultivate the power to form dispositions and habits through varied experience, not merely impart fixed responses. Examples contrast human infants (slow, variable learning that supports future flexibility) with chicks (rapid, fixed coordination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide social dependence and nurture as stimulus to growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Growth depends upon both the need for others and plasticity; prolonged infancy and continued dependence stimulate nurture, affection, foresight, and planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize environments that provide sustained care and social interaction; recognize that dependent, learning beings elicit nurturing practices that foster sympathetic watchfulness and intellectual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form active habits that control the environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A habit is a form of executive skill — an ability to use natural conditions as means to ends. True habits are active controls over the environment, not mere internal changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational aims should produce habits enabling economical and effective control of surroundings (walking, talking, professional skills). Emphasize habits as resources for future situations, not merely automatic reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish habituation (passive) from active, thoughtful habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Habituation is passive adjustment, an equilibrium of response to an environment one does not seek to change; active habits involve thoughtful readjustment to meet new conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid educating toward mere conformity or passive acquiescence. Use learning activities that require selection, discrimination, and intentional readjustment rather than passive repetition or mere getting 'used to' conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop intellectual and emotional dispositions as part of habit formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Habits include intellectual modes of thought, observation, reflection, and emotional inclinations — not just motor skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach so that habits incorporate understanding and desire: cultivate acquaintance with materials, ways of understanding situations, judgment, and reasoning along with skillful action (e.g., habits of mind that support professional competence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fixation and routine that arrest growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixity of habit can mean loss of freshness, open-mindedness, and originality; routine habits are unthinking and can sever intelligence from action, closing off plasticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counteract tendencies toward 'settling down' by ensuring the formation of habits involves active intelligence; reject methods relying solely on mechanical repetition to secure external efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the present as the locus of educative motive (reject preparation-as-main-spring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Education-as-preparation for a remote future weakens motive power, encourages procrastination, substitutes vague averages for individual judgment, and forces reliance on rewards and punishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make present experiences rich and significant so that present capacities are utilized; prepare for the future through improving present opportunities rather than treating schooling as mere training for later life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect immaturity while guiding — balance individuality and discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect the child's nature and see manifestations as signs of possible growth to be turned into means of development, not indulged for their own sake; training must both keep the child's nature and 'train off' undesirable traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid brushing aside distinctive individual traits as nuisances; provide time, insight, and character in teaching to both preserve natural impulses and direct them through knowledge and guidance (quotation of Emerson on respecting the child).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject 'unfolding toward a fixed goal' model of development
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unfolding' conception treats development as realization of a latent, fixed ideal or Absolute and thereby sets an immobile end that depreciates present activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute an abstract, transcendental goal (or adult ideal) as the standard for immediate guidance. Beware of pedagogies that 'draw out' prescribed content to match an a priori ideal, which often become methods of external control and dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing adult-formulated symbolism or institutional dictation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes (e.g., Froebel's symbolism or Hegelian institutional stepladders) translate vague ideals into adult-controlled techniques or institutional conformity, which can dictate rather than nurture development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of techniques that treat sensible things as mere symbols of an abstract Whole and of institutional arrangements that demand obedience instead of fostering transformation. Aim for methods that genuinely engage the child's capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of 'formal discipline' as sole educational aim
rubrics_metrics.description: The formal-discipline theory holds that certain faculties (perception, attention, memory, reasoning, imagination) can be trained directly by repeated exercises; this short-cut assumes these powers already exist in crude form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of training faculties by rote repetition; prefer indirect cultivation of abilities through meaningful activities that form habits in context rather than isolated drills purported to strengthen abstract powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: School's role: organize powers to ensure lifelong learning
rubrics_metrics.description: The school's purpose is to organize powers so that education continues after leaving school; it should create inclination and capacity to learn from life itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design curricula and experiences that instill the inclination to learn and practical means for continued self-education, thereby making schooling the basis for ongoing growth rather than an endpoint.
